item.title: New data group to boost digital economy, AI
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
New data group to boost digital economy, AI China National Data Group Co, a new centrally administered State-owned enterprise, was officially inaugurated on Tuesday in the Xiong'an New Area in Hebei province, in a move aimed at accelerating the development and utilization of data resources and supporting the country's artificial intelligence ambitions. With its headquarters in Xiong'an, the group will specialize in developing and utilizing data resources, unlocking their economic value, supporting AI development and fostering a more vibrant data industry. Its establishment brings the total number of SOEs directly administered by the central government to 100. Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang attended the inauguration ceremony and unveiled the plaque for the new company. Ding said the establishment of the company was a major strategic decision made by the Communist Party of China Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core, and will help China seize opportunities in AI development, accelerate the building of a digital China and forge new competitive advantages. He called for efforts to build the company into a world-class data technology enterprise. Ding urged the group to balance development and security, expand data-related services, accelerate the construction of data infrastructure and make breakthroughs in key and core technologies. He also stressed the need to improve corporate governance, establish sound operational and management mechanisms, and strengthen cooperation among government departments, local authorities and enterprises to support the development of the data industry. The new company is jointly funded and established by the State Council, the Xiong'an New Area Administrative Committee, China Telecom, China Unicom, China Mobile, State Grid Corp of China and China Southern Power Grid. Jian Qin, former general manager of China Unicom, is chairman of the group, while Chen Ronghui, former deputy head of the National Data Administration, has been appointed general manager. According to the company, it is positioned as a national team for data services, a leader in data infrastructure connectivity and a strategic force for national data science and technology innovation. Under the guidance of relevant government departments, it will strengthen coordination between central and local authorities and deepen cooperation across the data industry, promoting the sharing of resources and expertise and the joint development of business opportunities. Zhang Xianghong, a member of the national data expert advisory committee, said the new group will develop, integrate and operate national-level data resources through market-oriented and professional mechanisms. "The group will promote the cross-industry and cross-regional flow and sharing of data resources, significantly improve the efficiency of data allocation and break down 'data silos'," Zhang said, adding that it would help accelerate the construction of a unified national data market. The establishment of the company is a pioneering move globally that will strengthen China's competitiveness in data resources, he added. The nation has been seeking to make data held by government departments, companies and industries easier to share and use, while maintaining control over security and privacy. The push has gained urgency as the rapid development of generative AI increases demand for large volumes of high-quality data. China established the National Data Administration in 2023. Zhang said the administration and the new group will play distinct roles, with the regulator focusing on basic data rules and policy design and the company concentrating on the development and market-oriented operation of data resources. He said the changes will help improve the connectivity of data infrastructure, lower barriers so that more market participants have access to high-value data resources, and foster data innovation hubs, bringing together technology, industries and talent.

item.title: Houthis launch fresh strikes on Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
Houthis launch fresh strikes on Saudi Arabia Tensions flare up as security concerns prompt delay of Riyadh flagship event RIYADH/SANAA — Yemen's Houthi group said on Monday it had carried out six attacks against oil, aviation and military targets in Saudi Arabia over the past 48 hours, as security concerns prompted the kingdom to postpone its flagship investment conference originally scheduled for later this month. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement that the first attack targeted facilities of Saudi oil giant Aramco in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, claiming the strikes hit the targets and caused fires. The second targeted the Shaybah oil field in eastern Saudi Arabia and caused fires, he said. Other attacks targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Abha International Airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia, radar installations at Jabal Al-Hisn and Jabal Al-Rahmah, King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait, a Saudi naval task force camp, and a radar installation in the southern Najran region, he said. The six operations were in response to more than 200 Saudi air and missile strikes on Sanaa and other Houthi-held areas of Yemen over the past 48 hours, he said. There was no immediate comment on these operations from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition. Deadly strikes by Houthis in recent weeks have dealt a blow to the kingdom, forcing the airport to close until further notice and a slate of events to be postponed or canceled, including its flagship investment forum dubbed "Davos in the Desert". The kingdom announced on Monday the postponement of the 10th edition of the Future Investment Initiative conference, its flagship event originally scheduled for Oct 26-29 in Riyadh, to 2027. For nearly a decade, the conference has been a showcase for Saudi Arabia's push to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state — and to showcase its economic vision. Domestic airlines have scrambled to find alternative routes for the capital's 7 million residents, with recent targeted advertisements highlighting flights from Al-Qassim International Airport three hours from Riyadh. Government agencies in the Saudi capital have told employees to work from home starting from Monday, one worker and two consultants told AFP. The 99-story Kingdom Centre skyscraper in downtown Riyadh housing the regional office of the International Monetary Fund has also asked its employees to work from home. Attacks condemned The latest disruptions came amid continued cross-border attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, alongside heavy fighting between the group and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. A Houthi missile attack on a government military base in Yemen's southeastern oil-rich province of Shabwa earlier on Monday killed 73 people, with more than 200 others injured, local officials said. On Monday, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud discussed regional developments in separate phone calls with his Turkish and United Arab Emirates counterparts, during which they condemned the continued attacks by the Houthi group, the Saudi Press Agency reported. Britain announced on Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia against the Houthis to include "defensive" air patrols by Royal Air Force jets. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Royal Air Force Typhoon jets will help to "protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure from Houthi attack". Turkiye has sent the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a defense pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, to parliament to be ratified, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday. Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, who is in Kyrgyzstan at the moment, will submit the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission after returning to Turkiye, two of the sources said. Meanwhile, Egypt's parliament postponed a vote on authorizing military support for Saudi Arabia until Oct 26, after several lawmakers reportedly requested to speak. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi on Saturday asked parliament to authorize Egypt to defend Saudi Arabia if requested, while stressing he meant "defense", not war. Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. As Houthis intensified their attacks and as tensions flared up between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. The officials did not provide further details about the meeting, first reported by Axios. The Pentagon declined to comment. The Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. XINHUA-AGENCIES

item.title: A telling year reveals Takaichi's true colors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
A telling year reveals Takaichi's true colors: China Daily editorial As Japan and the United States began the so-called Keen Sword 27 large-scale joint military exercises across multiple locations in southwestern Japan on Monday, protests erupted in Japan against what is seen as an acceleration of the march toward war. It was against this backdrop that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Wednesday marked an awkward first anniversary in office. She ought to have been prepared for such an atmosphere. She knows full well how, over her first year in office, her government has harmed the interests of the Japanese people, damaged Japan's national reputation and undermined the prospects for peace and stability in the region by paving the way for the rise of neo-militarism in Japan. For Takaichi, the real error is not having erred; it is knowing the error and refusing to correct it. The international community is watching, and it has every reason to remain vigilant against the historical revisionism, geopolitical opportunism, political adventurism, narrow nationalism and social obscurantism that the Takaichi government is fostering in Japan. In a television program aired on Monday, Takaichi's predecessor, former prime minister Shigeru Ishiba criticized the Takaichi government and Japan's right-wing forces for their "dishonesty" toward history. Ishiba noted that it was Japan that started the war, causing tens of millions of deaths. He questioned how Japan can speak of "friendship", "equality" or "cooperation" with China if it cannot acknowledge these basic historical facts. Ishiba concluded that a nation so dishonest about history cannot establish solid diplomatic relations. Masahiko Shimizu, a constitutional law professor at Nippon Sport Science University, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CGTN last week. He criticized Japan for its failure to fully reflect on its history of aggression and its continued glorification of militarism. Since assuming office as Japan's first female prime minister on Oct 21 last year, Takaichi's tenure has not been a cause for celebration. Instead, it marks a year in which Japan has moved further down the path of neo-militarism, threatening regional security, eroding the postwar international order, and inflicting real costs on the Japanese economy and the Japanese people. Takaichi made an offering to the "war-criminal shrine" on Saturday in her official capacity as prime minister, and sent a monetary offering to it on Monday, despite strong opposition from neighboring countries. To all peace-loving people, Japanese politicians' repeated homages and visits to the shrine are an unmistakable signal that they refuse to honestly confront Japan's past aggression. Despite the "justifications" offered by Takaichi and her Cabinet for their tributes to the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, where 14 convicted Japanese Class-A war criminals from World War II are "honored", they cannot conceal their true intentions of rehabilitating war criminals, covering up wartime crimes, distorting historical facts and accelerating Japan's remilitarization. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning stressed that such acts expose the deep-rooted misconceptions of Japanese politicians regarding historical issues and their sinister attempt to exonerate war criminals, reverse the verdict on aggression, and pave the way for remilitarization. Making China's position clear, Mao said that China firmly opposes and strongly condemns Japan's moves concerning the Yasukuni Shrine and has lodged stern representations and strong protests. Apart from worsening ties with regional countries, the wrong trajectory on which Takaichi is leading Japan has also come at a high cost domestically. Japan's defense budget for fiscal 2026 has surpassed 9 trillion yen ($57 billion), the 14th consecutive annual increase and the fastest expansion in the postwar era. Meanwhile, ordinary Japanese face rising prices of food and utilities. Growing concerns over a Cabinet scandal of vote-buying, economic pressures, doubts about the fiscal deficit caused by a consumption tax cut and scrutiny of her beggar-thy-neighbor policy are all reflected in Takaichi's falling approval rating. Japan's neo-militarists know exactly what they are doing: steering the country toward another abyss of war. Takaichi has sharply accelerated that drift in her first year. Since Japan's war machine led to a regional catastrophe in WWII, the question now is how much longer the nation will give her to repeat the grave mistake.

RIZHAO, Shandong -- China launched a rocket from the ocean waters near the city of Rizhao in East China's Shandong province on Wednesday, placing a new satellite into planned orbit. item.title: Long March memories live on through village traditions in Gansu
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
Long March memories live on through village traditions in Gansu Ninety years ago, during the Long March, the First and Fourth Front Armies of the Red Army joined forces in Huining county, Gansu province. In the county's Hongbuzi village, residents provided the soldiers with grain and other supplies. The soldiers left IOUs for the grain they took, promising to repay the villagers after the revolution — a gesture that reflected the Red Army's emphasis on maintaining close ties with the people. That memory has been passed down through generations in Hongbuzi, where the Long March spirit of relying on and supporting the people remains part of the local heritage. In neighboring Tuoying village, residents have brought the story to life through a modern Qinqiang Opera performance, using a traditional Chinese theatrical form to share the history with new audiences. Since June 2021, the local folk orchestra has staged 116 performances, reaching an audience of 289,000. As gongs and drums ring out onstage, the story of the Red Army and its ties with local communities continues to reach new generations.

item.title: US crackdown on tech counterproductive
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
US crackdown on tech counterproductive: China Daily editorial The sanctions and bans imposed by the United States on Chinese technology are seemingly never-ending. In its latest move in the escalating crackdown on China's high-tech sector, the US administration has ordered the removal of all artificial intelligence technology developed by the Chinese company DeepSeek from the IT systems of civilian federal agencies. Announced by the US Department of Homeland Security on Monday, the order bans the use of DeepSeek's AI within civilian government agencies, as well as any technologies developed with the assistance of its models. The department baselessly cited "multiple threat vectors" associated with DeepSeek's models. Several US agencies, including the US Department of Commerce and the Navy, have already banned DeepSeek on government devices. The ban coincides with the US State Department's announcement on Monday of sweeping sanctions under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 against five Chinese entities suspected of "stealing trade secrets" from US companies. Additionally, the US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of all new models of Chinese drones and Chinese-made consumer routers last December. These synchronized moves reflect a broader strategy to gradually "decouple" US technological infrastructure from Chinese technology where the US thinks it is necessary. Under the pretext of safeguarding "national security" and protecting "intellectual property" from foreign "threats", Washington aims to slow down China's AI advances to maintain the US' competitiveness in the global technology arena. In today's world, technological competition is in fact competition between innovation ecosystems. If the US cannot shake China's comprehensive innovation ecosystem, then cracking down on individual technologies and applications will not hold back China's overall technological progress. Chinese AI companies have achieved breakthroughs in model algorithms and technological applications through dedicated research and development within such an innovation ecosystem. Groundless accusations that their success stems from "unfairly acquired technological strengths" are pure slander. For instance, DeepSeek's success can be attributed to its cost efficiency and open-source accessibility. Incorporating DeepSeek into projects costs companies and AI developers only a fraction of what they would pay for a closed-source model like Google's Gemini or Anthropic's Claude. This affordability is why DeepSeek's AI models are widely used by US tech companies and why its free chatbot is among the most downloaded apps in many countries and regions. The US' attempt to maintain its technological dominance through protectionism and administrative intervention is symptomatic of its strategic anxiety. Building technological barriers reflects a zero-sum mindset that is fundamentally at odds with the open, inclusive and mutually beneficial future of global AI development. Healthy high-tech competition drives innovation, while confrontation and "small yard, high fence" policies only hinder collaborative innovation and fragment supply chains without delivering real benefits. Moreover, the recent US actions against DeepSeek contradict the spirit of the consensus reached between the two sides last month, when they agreed on the establishment of the China-US AI Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI, with the next exchange scheduled in November. They also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents. The consensus was hard-won and should be translated into action and results. No country can address global challenges such as data security and algorithmic risks on its own. China and the US, both major countries in AI, should have the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people. To that end, the US should abandon its outdated Cold War mentality, respect independent innovations, and leverage the agreed communication channels to manage risks and resolve differences through dialogue.

item.title: Measures set to stabilize finance market
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
Measures set to stabilize finance market Move to enhance liquidity support, facilitate cross-border investment China's top financial regulators pledged on Monday to strengthen financial market stability amid rising global volatility while advancing the sector's opening-up, unveiling a series of measures to enhance liquidity support and facilitate cross-border investment. Speaking at the opening of the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing, Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, said maintaining capital market stability remains a top priority, warning of growing spillover risks as volatility across global equity, bond and foreign exchange markets becomes increasingly interconnected. To strengthen market resilience, the CSRC will improve long-term performance assessment mechanisms for institutional investors, broaden channels for medium and long-term capital inflows and deepen mutual fund reforms. The regulator approved the registration of the country's first batch of 18 actively managed exchange-traded funds on Monday, a move Wu said will bring additional capital into the market. Listed companies will be encouraged to increase share buybacks and purchases by major shareholders, Wu said, while calling for heightened vigilance against leveraged products traded overseas that are linked to individual A-share stocks. Also at the opening, Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, announced plans to establish a liquidity backstop for large-scale redemptions by nonbank financial institutions, as a new macroprudential tool to stabilize the bond market. The facility would be activated under specific circumstances when asset managers face widespread liquidity stress and bond markets enter a negative feedback loop of redemptions and forced selling, while balancing systemic risk prevention against moral hazard. Eligible institutions will include bank wealth management subsidiaries, mutual fund managers and their parent banks or securities firms, Pan said. On financial opening-up, Pan said the PBOC will expand access to its standing lending facility — a monetary policy tool that provides collateralized financing to meet temporary liquidity needs — to cover all domestic deposit-taking financial institutions, including locally incorporated foreign banks. Pan said the central bank will roll out a pilot to allow overseas financial institutions to participate in renminbi trading in China's interbank foreign exchange market and extend access to its RMB repo facility — aimed at helping specific overseas institutions obtain yuan liquidity — to foreign-funded RMB clearing banks. Wu said the CSRC will facilitate investment under the Qualified Foreign Institutional Investor scheme, support domestic and international institutions in collaborating to launch more index products based on Chinese financial assets, and accelerate efforts to include RMB-denominated stock trading counters and real estate investment trusts in the Stock Connect programs. Ding Xiangqun, minister of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, pledged to deepen institutional opening-up, improve the regulatory environment for foreign institutions and encourage their participation in wealth management, pension and healthcare, and green finance. Zhu Hexin, head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, said the regulator will introduce a package of capital account foreign exchange reforms to facilitate enterprises' cross-border investment and financing, while expanding a pilot program allowing securities firms to conduct foreign exchange settlement and sales. Pan also outlined future monetary policy framework reforms, including studying a shift toward overnight operations as the mainstay of open market operations, making the overnight repo rate the principal policy rate. The PBOC will also promote more diversified loan pricing benchmarks beyond the loan prime rate and further phase out benchmark deposit and lending rates, while promoting connectivity between the interbank bond market and the exchange bond market, Pan added. Also on Monday, the PBOC, together with 10 other departments, rolled out a guideline on enhancing financial support for building global sci-tech innovation hubs in Beijing, Shanghai and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Zhang Linwan contributed to this story.

item.title: 'China Haul': Empty suitcases in, packed suitcases out
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
When a British woman suffering from hindered mobility following a stroke was able to discard her wheelchair and walk with the help of a Chinese-made exoskeleton robot at the China Import and Export Fair this week, she could barely hold back her tears. Her son, who was equally overwhelmed by what Chinese technology could achieve, decided to immediately place an order for the device. "I have never seen anything like this in the United Kingdom, or even in Europe," he said. The heartwarming moment was captured on camera, and the footage was widely circulated on social media. Rafael Saavedra, a Venezuelan vlogger attending the fair, described the scene as a glimpse into the future. "Here you can see, touch and test tomorrow's consumer technology — from robots that can run errands to massage chairs," he said. The scene was actually far from unique, as the viral "China Haul" trend has gripped the ongoing China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, which opened in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, on Oct 14 and runs through Nov 4. While influencers have popularized the "China Haul" hashtag on social media, visitors to the fair are buyers searching for China's next-generation products. Across the fair's exhibition halls, foreign visitors were captivated by artificial intelligence-based toys, humanoid robots and other smart devices, with some placing orders on the spot. Their shopping lists tell a broader story. After last year's boom in "China Travel" brought millions of overseas visitors to the country, the latest trend indicates that many are returning home with something more than intangible memories. They are packing their suitcases with Chinese brands — from tech products such as drones and foldable smartphones to lifestyle goods such as sports shoes and AI-powered toys. In other words, China's appeal is moving beyond affordability toward innovation, and that momentum is reflected in official figures. China recorded 23.72 million visa-free entries by foreign nationals from January to August, up 26.8 percent year-on-year, according to the National Immigration Administration. Data from the Ministry of Commerce shows that in the first seven months, overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan ($39.5 billion), an increase of 27.8 percent compared with the same period a year earlier. It underscores a steady recovery in inbound tourism and consumer spending. Speaking on Friday at a news conference in Beijing, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said that China will continue opening its doors wider, allowing more foreign visitors to better understand and appreciate the country through two-way exchanges. The growing enthusiasm for "China Haul" among visitors is also benefiting international retailers. According to Inditex, a global fashion retailer that owns brands including Zara and Massimo Dutti, the share of sales generated by overseas visitors at the Zara flagship store on Shanghai's Nanjing East Road and the Massimo Dutti store on Nanjing West Road has risen more than 10 percent year-on-year. The company attributed the increase in sales to the stores' central locations, the distinctive shopping experiences they offer, their assortment of products, and China's increasingly convenient departure tax refund policy. Taikoo Li, a popular commercial zone in Beijing's Sanlitun, reported a similar trend. The retail complex said the city's continued efforts to improve services for visitors, streamline tax refund procedures and enhance cultural and tourism experiences are attracting more foreigners. "The number of overseas visitors to our complex has seen a clear upward trend," said CT Ma, general manager of Taikoo Li Sanlitun. "International shoppers are interested not only in global luxury brands, but also in Chinese brands that combine local cultural elements with contemporary design. Sportswear, lifestyle products and brands with distinctive Chinese characteristics have become particularly popular," he said. "They are no longer coming only to see China. They are coming to discover what China makes, what China designs and, increasingly, what China creates," Ma said.
